title: HE TORE A LION APART WITH HIS BARE HANDS… BUT WHAT HE FOUND INSIDE ITS DEAD BODY WAS EVEN MORE SHOCKING.
paragraphs: HE TORE A LION APART WITH HIS BARE HANDS… BUT WHAT HE FOUND INSIDE ITS DEAD BODY WAS EVEN MORE SHOCKING.

The lion was dead. The honey was real. But the greatest revelation in Samson’s story isn't about strength or sweetness. It's about the danger of a powerful man who could defeat what attacked him but struggled to defeat what was destroying him from within.

“And he took thereof in his hands, and went on eating, and came to his father and mother, and he gave them, and they did eat: but he told not them that he had taken the honey out of the carcase of the lion.” — Judges 14:9 (KJV)
There is something deeply unsettling about a man reaching into the remains of something that once tried to kill him… and pulling out something sweet.
A lion had roared against him.
Its jaws were powerful enough to crush bone. Its claws were sharp enough to tear flesh. Its attack could have ended his life in seconds.
But the lion died.
And sometime later, when the man returned to the place where the animal had fallen, he discovered something he never expected.
Honey.
Not beside the lion.
Not hanging from a nearby tree.
Inside the carcass of the very beast that had tried to destroy him.
But before you turn this into a beautiful little message about how God brings sweetness out of suffering, there is something you need to know.
The man who killed that lion would eventually lose his freedom, his eyesight, and his life.
And the same man who was strong enough to tear apart a lion would later become helpless in the hands of his enemies.
How?
How does someone experience the supernatural power of God and still walk toward personal destruction?
How does a man defeat a lion with his bare hands yet fail to recognize the danger growing inside his own heart?
And what does any of this have to do with the secret battles you are fighting right now?
Stay with this story.
Because the honey is not the most disturbing part.
The silence is.
And somewhere between that dead lion, that hidden honey, and a Savior who would come centuries later, there is a truth about grace that every struggling believer needs to hear.
Samson was not an ordinary man.

Before he was born, an angel of the LORD announced that he would be set apart to God from the womb. His mother was instructed concerning his consecration, and the child was to begin delivering Israel from the Philistines (Judges 13:3–5).
His calling began before his first breath.
But having a calling does not automatically mean a person will always make wise choices.
That distinction matters.
Because some of the most heartbreaking stories in Scripture belong to people who were genuinely used by God yet made decisions that brought terrible consequences.
Samson was one of them.
Judges 14 opens with Samson going down to Timnah, where he saw a Philistine woman and wanted to marry her.
His parents questioned the decision.
Samson insisted.
He wanted what he wanted.

And although Judges 14:4 reveals that God was working through these events to confront the Philistines, that divine purpose does not mean every desire, attitude, or decision Samson displayed was morally right.
God's sovereignty is not the same thing as God's approval.
That is an important truth for anyone who has ever confused an open door with divine permission.
Sometimes we become so determined to pursue something that we stop asking whether our hearts are aligned with the Lord.
We want the relationship.
We want the opportunity.
We want the pleasure.
We want the outcome.
And when someone who loves us raises a concern, we call it interference.
When Scripture challenges our desires, we search for a more comfortable interpretation.
When conviction interrupts us, we convince ourselves that everything will work out.
But not everything we can pursue is something we should pursue.
And not every path that appears exciting leads somewhere safe.
As Samson traveled toward Timnah with his parents, he encountered something terrifying.
Judges 14:5 says that a young lion came roaring against him near the vineyards of Timnah.
Imagine that moment.
The sudden movement.
The violent sound.
The terrible realization that a predator was charging toward him.
No sword is mentioned in Samson's hand.
No spear.
No shield.
No army standing behind him.
And then Scripture records something extraordinary.
“And the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him, and he rent him as he would have rent a kid, and he had nothing in his hand.” — Judges 14:6 (KJV)
The Hebrew text begins its description of the Spirit's action with the words:
וַתִּצְלַח עָלָיו רוּחַ יְהוָה
Vattitslach alav ruach YHWH.
The phrase communicates that the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon Samson.
The Hebrew verb used here, from tsalach (צָלַח), describes the Spirit's powerful action upon him in this context.
This was not merely an impressive demonstration of physical strength.
The biblical writer deliberately identifies the source of Samson's extraordinary ability.
The Spirit of the LORD empowered him.
Samson tore the lion apart.
And then something surprising happened.
He kept the incident from his parents.
Judges 14:6 says he did not tell his father or mother what he had done.
Scripture does not explicitly tell us why he remained silent, and we should not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
But the detail becomes significant as the story unfolds.
Because this will not be the last time Samson keeps something important from the people closest to him.
Some time later, Samson returned to marry the woman.
And as he traveled, he turned aside to look at the lion's remains.
There, in the carcass, he discovered a swarm of bees and honey.
The Hebrew of Judges 14:8 describes the discovery with the words:
עֲדַת דְּבֹרִים בִּגְוִיַּת הָאַרְיֵה וּדְבָשׁ
Adat devorim bigviyat ha'aryeh udevash.
A swarm or colony of bees in the lion's carcass, and honey.
It was an extraordinary sight.
Something associated with death had become the location of something sweet.
But we need to be careful here.
The Bible does not explicitly say that God placed the honey there as a promise that every painful experience will eventually produce a pleasant outcome.
Nor does the passage teach that the lion represents Satan or that the honey represents the Gospel.
Those may sound like compelling sermon illustrations, but they are not explanations the text itself gives us.
The honey becomes central to the riddle Samson later tells at his wedding feast.
And the circumstances surrounding its discovery raise serious questions about Samson's conduct.

As someone set apart under a Nazirite calling, Samson was connected to the consecration instructions of Numbers 6, which included restrictions concerning contact with the dead. Judges does not explicitly explain whether he touched the carcass itself, so we should not claim a proven violation on that detail alone.
What the passage does tell us is that Samson took the honey, ate it, gave some to his parents, and concealed where it came from.
He enjoyed the sweetness.
He shared the sweetness.
But he withheld the truth about its source.
And this is where the story begins to reach beyond ancient Timnah and into the uncomfortable realities of our own lives.
Because it is possible to enjoy something while refusing to examine what surrounds it.
It is possible to receive something that feels good without asking whether the way we obtained it was wise.
It is possible to look strong in public while privately entertaining choices that threaten our integrity.
And it is possible to tell people enough of our story to appear transparent while carefully hiding the details we do not want questioned.
Maybe you know what that feels like.
Maybe you have become skilled at saying, “I'm fine,” while quietly struggling with something you are afraid to confess.
Maybe people admire your faith because they see you serving, praying, posting Scripture, encouraging others, and showing up at church.
But they do not see what happens when the room is empty.
They do not know about the temptation you keep revisiting.
The resentment you keep feeding.
The relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
The bitterness you have learned to disguise as discernment.
The secret habit you promised God you would abandon.
The exhaustion you hide because everyone expects you to be strong.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that you have become so accustomed to carrying these things that you no longer recognize how heavy they are.
You can still smile.
Still worship.
Still encourage somebody else.
Still quote the right verses.
Still appear spiritually alive.
While something inside you is quietly falling apart.
Listen carefully.
Being used by God is not permission to ignore the condition of your heart.
That truth should humble every one of us.
Samson's strength was extraordinary.
But his strength did not make him immune to temptation.
His calling was real.
But his calling did not remove his responsibility to obey.
God's Spirit empowered him for particular acts of deliverance.
But that empowerment was not a guarantee that Samson would always exercise self-control.
And the rest of his story makes that painfully clear.
The man who tore apart a lion would eventually be betrayed through his relationship with Delilah.
The man whose enemies could not easily overpower him would be bound.
The man who once moved with astonishing strength would be forced to grind grain in prison.
And the man who had seen so much would have his eyes gouged out by the Philistines.
Judges 16:20 records one of the most devastating statements in Samson's life.
“And he wist not that the LORD was departed from him.” (KJV)
He did not know.
Those words should disturb us.
Not because every struggling Christian should fear that one failure means God has abandoned them. That is not what this passage teaches.
Samson lived in a particular period of Israel's history and experienced a particular Spirit-given empowerment connected to his calling.
The New Testament gives believers in Christ the assurance of God's faithfulness and the sealing of the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13–14).
But Samson's experience still warns us about the danger of spiritual presumption.
We can become so familiar with God's gifts that we begin to neglect God's commands.
So accustomed to yesterday's victories that we stop examining today's compromises.
So confident in our ability to withstand temptation that we ignore the first steps leading toward it.
And sometimes the most dangerous sentence a believer can speak is not “I am struggling.”
It is “I can handle this.”
Because confession recognizes a need for grace.
Pride denies the danger.
The apostle Paul would later write:
Perhaps you have been fighting a lion everyone can see while ignoring a temptation nobody knows about.
You have been battling financial pressure, family problems, grief, rejection, betrayal, or disappointment.
And those battles are real.
They hurt.
They exhaust you.
They sometimes make it difficult to get out of bed and face another day.
But while you are trying to survive what is happening around you, have you paid attention to what is happening within you?
Has suffering made you more dependent on Christ, or have you begun using your pain to justify choices you once knew were wrong?
Has disappointment brought you into honest prayer, or has it slowly hardened your heart?
Has loneliness drawn you toward healthy Christian community, or toward secrecy?
These are not questions meant to condemn the wounded.
They are invitations to bring our whole lives into the light of Christ.
Because Jesus does not merely care about the battles that threaten us from the outside.
He cares about the sins, wounds, fears, and desires shaping us on the inside.
And He is not afraid of what He finds there.
There is another detail in Samson's story that makes the lion and the honey even more significant.
At the wedding feast, Samson turned the discovery into a riddle.
“Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness.” — Judges 14:14 (KJV)
In the language of the King James Version, “meat” here means food.
The Hebrew says:
מֵהָאֹכֵל יָצָא מַאֲכָל וּמֵעַז יָצָא מָתוֹק
Meha'okhel yatza ma'akhal, ume'az yatza matok.
“Out of the eater came food, and out of the strong came sweetness.”
The riddle depends on the unusual reversal Samson witnessed.
The predator had become the location of food.
The powerful beast had become associated with sweetness.
But the riddle also became part of a deeply troubled wedding celebration marked by threats, manipulation, anger, and violence.
The story is not a simple inspirational account of a strong man discovering a blessing.
It is part of a larger narrative about a gifted, complicated, frequently impulsive man through whom God nevertheless advanced His purposes against Israel's oppressors.
And that complexity matters.
Because the Bible is not interested in protecting the reputations of its human heroes by hiding their failures.
It tells us the truth.
Abraham believed God, yet he also acted out of fear.
David was a man after God's own heart, yet he committed grievous sin.
Peter loved Jesus, yet denied knowing Him.
Samson was empowered by the Spirit, yet repeatedly made destructive choices.
Scripture does not present these men as flawless saviors.
It reveals how desperately humanity needs the One who is.
Jesus Christ.
And here is where the story becomes greater than the lion.
Greater than the honey.
Greater than Samson's strength.
Because Samson's life ultimately forces us to confront the limits of human deliverers.
He could tear apart a lion.
But he could not save himself from his own sin.
He could defeat enemies.
But he could not become the sinless Redeemer Israel truly needed.
He could begin delivering Israel from the Philistines.
But he could not deliver humanity from the power and penalty of sin.
For that, we needed someone greater.
We needed Jesus.
And the difference between Samson and Jesus is breathtaking.
Samson was empowered by God's Spirit, yet morally imperfect.
Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
Samson's strength was used in violent confrontations with Israel's enemies.
Jesus demonstrated His authority over sin, death, demons, disease, and the grave.
Samson's story ends with his death in the collapse of a Philistine temple.
Jesus willingly gave His life on the cross, rose bodily from the dead on the third day, and lives forever.
Samson's final act brought judgment upon his enemies.
Christ's saving work provides forgiveness and reconciliation to all who repent and believe in Him.
And while Samson's riddle speaks of sweetness coming from the remains of a dead lion, the Gospel announces something infinitely greater.
Life came through the death and resurrection of the sinless Son of God.
Not because the honey in Judges 14 was secretly a prediction of the cross.
But because the whole biblical story directs our attention beyond imperfect deliverers toward the perfect Savior.
Jesus did not simply survive death.
He conquered it.
He did not merely escape the power of sin.
He bore the penalty of sin for His people.
He did not simply give us a temporary victory over an earthly enemy.
He opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
And what He accomplished cannot be reduced to a motivational saying about turning pain into purpose.
It is redemption.
It is grace.
It is the Gospel.
The Greek New Testament uses a beautiful word for grace:
χάρις — charis.
Grace.
God's undeserved favor.
In Ephesians 2:8–9, Paul declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (KJV)
The Greek phrase τῇ γὰρ χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι διὰ πίστεως expresses the truth that salvation is by grace through faith.
Not by our strength.
Not by our religious reputation.
Not by the number of battles we have won.
Not by our ability to conceal our weaknesses.
Not by our giving.
Not by our achievements.
By grace.
Through faith.
Because of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps this is what you most need to hear today.
You do not have to pretend you are stronger than you really are.
You do not have to perform spiritual perfection to approach the Savior.
You do not have to hide your failures behind religious language.
You do not have to wait until you have repaired every broken part of your life before crying out for mercy.
Christ calls sinners to repentance.
And His grace is sufficient for those who come to Him in faith.
That does not mean repentance is optional.
It does not mean sin is harmless.
It does not mean grace gives us permission to continue embracing what Christ died to save us from.
Romans 6:1–2 rejects that very idea.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace is God's undeserved kindness that saves us and teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 makes that clear.
And 1 John 1:9 gives struggling believers a promise worth holding onto:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Read that again.
Not “If we successfully hide our sins.”
Not “If we convince everyone we are doing well.”
Not “If we promise never to struggle again.”
If we confess our sins.
There is a kind of freedom that begins when we stop defending what God is calling us to surrender.
When we stop pretending.
When we finally say, “Lord, I need You here too.”
In the anger.
In the addiction.
In the jealousy.
In the bitterness.
In the shame.
In the secret grief.
In the temptation we have been too embarrassed to name.
Jesus is not impressed by a polished version of us that refuses to tell the truth.
He calls us to come into His light.
And His light does not merely expose what is wrong.
It leads us toward the forgiveness, cleansing, and transformation we cannot manufacture ourselves.
Maybe your life has become a collection of contradictions.
You love God, yet you struggle.
You believe His Word, yet sometimes disobey it.
You want to forgive, yet the memory still hurts.
You want to trust Him, yet fear keeps returning.
You want to be faithful, yet you know how often your heart wanders.
Do not confuse those struggles with permission to surrender to sin.
But do not confuse them with proof that Christ cannot restore you either.
The answer is not to become better at hiding.
The answer is to bring the truth before God.
To repent where repentance is needed.
To seek help where help is needed.
To confess to trustworthy believers when secrecy has become a prison.
To return again and again to the Scriptures.
To remember that sanctification is not the achievement of self-sufficient people.
It is the work of God in those who belong to Christ.
And this is why the end of Samson's story matters so much.
In Judges 16, after his humiliation and imprisonment, Samson cried out to the LORD.
He asked God to remember him and strengthen him once more.
God granted him strength for his final act against the Philistines, although that act also cost Samson his life.
The passage is sobering.
It is not a promise that every consequence of sin will disappear when we pray.
Samson's eyes were not restored.
His imprisonment was not erased.
His life did not return to what it had been.
But even at the end of a deeply troubled life, Scripture records him calling upon the LORD.
And Hebrews 11:32 later includes Samson among those remembered in the testimony of faith.
That does not excuse his sins.
It reminds us that God's dealings with imperfect people are more profound than a simple division between impressive heroes and hopeless failures.
And if you are reading this with regret in your heart, please understand something.
Your past may have consequences.
Some relationships may require patient rebuilding.
Some wounds may take time to heal.
Some wrongs may require confession, restitution, or difficult changes.
And not every earthly loss can be reversed.
But your failure does not place you beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
The cross is not a reward for people who never fell.
It is the place where the sinless Savior gave Himself for sinners.
And His resurrection is the declaration that death does not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
That is why our message is not simply that broken people can become successful.
It is something far greater.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing the truth.
But by redeeming sinners who repent and believe, forgiving what they could never cleanse themselves, and transforming lives through the power of His Gospel.
Maybe the lion in your life has already fallen.
Maybe you survived something you thought would destroy you.
Maybe you are still standing after betrayal, grief, abandonment, or a season that nearly crushed your faith.
Give God thanks for sustaining you.
But do not assume that surviving one battle means you no longer need to guard your heart.
And maybe you are still in the middle of the fight.
Still praying through tears.
Still resisting temptation.
Still waiting for healing.
Still wondering why obedience feels so costly.
Do not measure God's love by how quickly your circumstances become sweet.
Measure His love by the cross of Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
There is your assurance.
Not a lion's carcass.
Not a handful of honey.
Not a temporary victory.
The crucified and risen Christ.
The One who loved sinners enough to die for them.
The One who calls us out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
The One who does not merely make our stories more inspiring.
He makes the spiritually dead alive by grace through faith.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Not for the sake of appearances.
Not so anyone can judge your answer.
But because somebody reading this may have been silently fighting a battle for months.
What is harder for you right now?
The lion attacking your life from the outside?
Or the struggle you have been hiding on the inside?
Let those words become a reminder of a real decision to seek God honestly, not a substitute for repentance or the help you may need.
Because somewhere in this community is another person who thinks they are the only one struggling.
And your simple act of honesty may encourage them to stop suffering in silence.
There is another way you can help this message reach someone who needs it.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
It doesn't.
But because someone in your circle may never open a Bible study, attend a church gathering, or ask for prayer publicly.
They may still read a message shared by someone they trust.
Someone you love may be losing hope.
Someone you know may be struggling with secret sin.
Someone in your family may have drifted away from Christ.
Someone who has never believed may be searching for answers.
And perhaps this article can become an invitation for them to open the Scriptures and discover Jesus for themselves.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who are uncertain about Christianity to join us.
Because this ministry is not about building a personality.
It is about making the truth of Jesus Christ known.
And if these messages have helped strengthen your faith, I want to invite you into something deeper.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible, encourage faithful discipleship, and help people become more firmly rooted in God's Word.
The Gospel is a gift of grace.
And that is what makes generous support meaningful.
It can be given freely, prayerfully, and joyfully.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
These items are not the heart of the mission.
Christ is.
But they can serve as reminders of biblical truth, opportunities for conversation, and practical expressions of encouragement.
The free Gospel resources are not reserved for those who can afford to give.
Your worth before God is not measured by your financial contribution.
A faithful ministry should never make someone feel that they must pay to be loved by God.
We give because He first loved us.
We serve because Christ has served us.
We share because the Gospel is too precious to keep to ourselves.
And as we come to the end of Samson's story, I want you to remember one final thing.
The lion was strong.
Samson was stronger than the lion because the Spirit of the LORD empowered him.
But Samson was never strong enough to become his own savior.
Neither are we.
And that is not the end of our hope.
It is the beginning of understanding why we need Jesus.
You may have conquered things that once terrified you.
You may have survived circumstances that nearly broke you.
You may have discovered unexpected kindness in seasons of terrible pain.
But none of those victories can take the place of the cross.
And none of your failures can make Christ's saving power insufficient for those who truly turn to Him.
So if you have been hiding, come into the light.
If you have been wandering, repent and return.
If you have been proud, humble yourself before God.
If you have been wounded, bring your pain to the Savior.
If you have been trying to save yourself through your own strength, put your trust in the One who died and rose again.
And if you are tired of pretending to be the strongest person in the room, remember that you were never meant to be your own redeemer.
You need Jesus.
We all do.
The lion and the honey may be what first captured your attention.
But I pray that when you close this article, the image you carry will not be a dead animal filled with honey.
It will be an empty tomb.
Because a lion's death became the setting for Samson's strange discovery.
But Christ's death and resurrection accomplished something no human strength could ever achieve.
The salvation of sinners.
And that is a sweetness greater than anything Samson ever tasted.
You may have survived the lion that came to destroy you—but only Jesus can save the soul you were never strong enough to rescue.
